tagline.text: A marble town and twin forts guarding a blue bay

items.credit: Carlo Joseph Moskito / CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: The capital island of Romblon province, floating in the middle of the Sibuyan Sea and one of the Philippines' leading marble-producing areas. From the Bonbon Beach sandbar, where a path opens across the sea at low tide, to 1640s Spanish forts, a coral-stone cathedral, and quiet macro diving, you can enjoy the relaxed pace of an old port town with few tourists.

Romblon province is made up of more than 20 islands scattered across the Sibuyan Sea between Luzon and the Visayas. The largest is Tablas Island, and the one with the highest mountain is Sibuyan Island. Romblon Island sits between the two, a small island of about 87 km², entirely occupied by the town of Romblon, which shares its name with the province and serves as the provincial capital. The port and town center sit deep inside a bay ringed by green hills, so the scenery is inviting from the moment your boat sails in.

Marble defines this island. White, green, pink, and black marble is quarried from mountains all across the island, making Romblon one of the Philippines' foremost marble-producing areas, and roadside workshops carve and sell marble mortars, statues, and tableware. Piles of white stone dust outside these workshops are a sight unique to the island.

Traces of the Spanish era are also clear. Fort San Andres and Fort Santiago, built on hills on either side of the bay in the 1640s to guard against Moro pirates and Dutch fleets, face each other across the water, and in the middle of town stands St. Joseph Cathedral, built of coral stone and completed around 1726. Both the forts and the cathedral are designated National Cultural Treasures.

Along the west coast, Bonbon Beach, where a sandbar emerges to a small island offshore at low tide, is followed by quiet beach villages, and Cobrador Island and Logbon Island offshore are explored on hopping tours. With no big resorts and few tourists, it suits travelers who want a few quiet days near Boracay, or anyone wanting to combine a historical stroll with the beach.
A white sand beach in Lonos village; at low tide, a sand path opens all the way to a small island offshore. It's about
10–15 minutes
from town by tricycle, and the sunset view is especially beautiful.

blocks.title: Twin Forts San Andres and Santiago

children.text: 1640s stone forts facing each other on hills on either side of the bay. Climb up to Fort San Andres for a sweeping view of the red-roofed town, the port, and the islands offshore.
A coral-stone church built from
to
, one of the oldest churches in the Philippines. Its bell tower and the plaza fountain nearby give the old town its atmosphere.
Workshops that cut and polish marble line the road around the island. Watch the process at work and pick up a small mortar or carving as a souvenir.
Small islands northwest of Romblon Island, with white sand beaches and clear water good for snorkeling and picnics. Cobrador Island also has a cave with traces of ancient burials.

The waters off Romblon are rich in small creatures like nudibranchs, coconut octopuses, and seahorses, making it a macro diving spot popular with underwater photographers. Trial dives are also available at dive resorts on the island.
Ride a motorbike or tricycle around the roughly
40km
road circling the island, passing quiet beaches, marble quarries, and hilltop wind turbines.

items.title: Day 1
items.subtitle: Arrival and a walk around town

children.text: Arrive at Romblon port on the overnight boat from Batangas, check in and rest
Visit St. Joseph Cathedral, the plaza, and the old municipal hall
Climb Fort San Andres to enjoy the view of the town and the bay
Walk the sandbar and watch the sunset at Bonbon Beach
Charter a bangka for island hopping to Cobrador and Logbon Islands, with snorkeling and a beach lunch
Rest at your lodging, or try a trial dive at a dive resort
Seafood dinner at a restaurant by the port
Ride a motorbike or tricycle around the island, visiting marble workshops and quarries
Stop by Fort Santiago and the quiet beaches to the south
Travel on to Sibuyan or Tablas Island, or board the boat back to Batangas
If you have more time, it's also worth crossing by boat to Sibuyan Island to combine Mount Guiting-Guiting and its waterfalls into a wider tour of Romblon province's islands.
The simplest way from Manila is to take the overnight RORO ferry from Batangas port to Romblon town. Montenegro Shipping and others depart in the evening and arrive at dawn, about
8–10 hours
, for a regular-seat fare of around
. Return sailings often run only on certain days of the week, so check the schedule before planning your trip. From Manila to Batangas port takes about
2–3 hours
by bus.
A small Cebu Pacific-affiliated plane flies a few times a week from Manila to Tugdan Airport (TBH) in Alcantara, Tablas Island, taking about
1 hour
. From the airport, travel by van or tricycle to San Agustin Port in northeastern Tablas, about
1 hour–1 hour 30 minutes
, then take a boat to Romblon Island, about
1–2 hours
, for around
. Flights are infrequent, so you'll need to coordinate the flight and boat schedules together.
Boats also run between Magdiwang and San Fernando ports on Sibuyan Island and Romblon Island, taking about
1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours

. Coming from Boracay, you can take a boat from Caticlan to Santa Fe in southern Tablas, then travel overland up to San Agustin to change boats, though this takes a full day. Small boat routes change often with the season and weather, so check the latest schedule.
Town is walkable, and a tricycle to Bonbon Beach costs about
one way. For touring the island, a chartered tricycle (about
for half a day to a full day) or a rented motorbike (about
per day) is convenient, and an island-hopping bangka can be chartered for about
December–May
is the dry season and the best time for island hopping and walking the sandbar.
March–May
brings the calmest seas and clearest water, with good visibility for snorkeling and diving, and midday temperatures around
. During
December–February

, the northeast monsoon can roughen the sea on the island's east side, though the west side and inside the bay stay relatively calm. In January, the Biniray Festival, a sea procession honoring the Santo Niño, fills the town with crowds.
June–November

is the wet season, affected by the southwest monsoon and typhoons. The Sibuyan Sea is a frequent typhoon path, and boats linking Batangas and Tablas can be suspended for several days at a time during this period. If traveling in the wet season, it's safer to keep at least one spare day before your return.

Lodging clusters around the town near the port and cathedral, and around Lonos, home to Bonbon Beach. Town pensions and small hotels run about
a night, making them convenient even if you arrive on the dawn boat. For the beach, the resorts and dive resorts in Lonos and along the island's west coast are good, running about
a night. Rooms are limited, so book ahead for long weekends and the January festival.

Food centers on seafood caught fresh from the sea. Restaurants by the port and carinderias around the market commonly serve grilled fish, kinilaw (fish cured in vinegar and ginger), and crab and shrimp simmered in coconut milk, and a meal costs about

. In the morning, try a local breakfast of freshly baked pandesal bread with hot tsokolate (cocoa drink) from the market. In the evening, some stalls around the plaza sell grilled skewers, and there are a few Western-style cafés in town.
The Bonbon Beach sandbar only appears at low tide. Check the tide chart, and head back to the beach as soon as the water starts coming in.
Boats to Batangas often don't run daily, so if your return date is fixed, check the return sailing first before setting your arrival date.
There are a few ATMs in town, but they sometimes break down or run out of cash, so it's safer to bring the cash you'll need in advance.
Marble souvenirs are heavy. Choose small carvings or coasters, and for larger pieces, ask the workshop about packing and shipping.
Fort San Andres has many steps and little shade, so it's best to climb it in the early morning or late afternoon.
The air-conditioned berths on the overnight boat can get cold, so bring long sleeves, and keep valuables on your person.
If combining this with a trip to Sibuyan Island, it's more efficient to visit Romblon Island first, then take the boat straight to Manila from Sibuyan.

All boats to Romblon are heavily affected by weather. When a typhoon warning or strong wind advisory is issued, the coast guard suspends departures, so check the latest notices from the shipping line and coast guard before you set out.
The sandbar and coral areas have many sea urchins and sharp shells, so wear aqua shoes.
Near marble workshops and quarries, stone dust and cutting machinery are hazardous, so don't enter work areas without permission.
When island hopping on a small bangka, always wear a life jacket, and plan to return before the afternoon winds pick up.
The island has no major hospital, so emergencies require transfer to Manila or Tablas. Bring basic medicine and travel insurance.
The cathedral and forts are cultural heritage sites, so don't climb the walls or write graffiti, and view them quietly during Mass.
About
1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours
from Romblon Island by boat, this is the "Galapagos of the Philippines," with old-growth forest covering Mount Guiting-Guiting and clear waterfalls and rivers.
At the southern tip of Romblon province, just north of Boracay, this island is known for white sand beaches and cliff diving. Getting there via Tablas takes a full day.
The Philippines' foremost beach resort, connected by boat between Santa Fe on Tablas Island and Caticlan — a good pairing with Romblon Island for a contrast of quiet and liveliness.
A heart-shaped island across the Sibuyan Sea to the north, known for the Holy Week Moriones Festival and its fortress church. Boat schedules vary by season, so check in advance.
